newsitem.title: UK: Hague, boy wonder, becomes Conservative leader.
newsitem.headline: Hague, boy wonder, becomes Conservative leader.

text.p: To his supporters William Hague is the new face desperately needed by their battered Conservative Party, a boy wonder who, at 36, can dilute the "Blair effect" that has swept Britain since Labour took power on May 1.
But the doubters say the Conservatives may have made a terrible mistake in electing Hague as leader on Thursday, effectively moving from Major to minor.

They claim members of parliament have chosen a man of little experience, nicknamed "Hague the vague" because of his fuzzy political beliefs, who may continue the mistakes of his predecessor, John Major.

Hague is the youngest Conservative leader since the late 18th century and eight years younger than Prime Minister Tony Blair who ended 18 years of Conservative rule with a landslide election victory on May 1.

The 92 members of parliament who voted for Hague rather than former finance minister Kenneth Clarke in the third and final round believe Hague provides a double advantage to a party still licking its wounds after its election thrashing.
He cancels out the youthful image of Blair, 44, and marks a distinct break from the "old" Conservative government.

"We must take this once in a lifetime opportunity to make a fresh start -- a fresh start in our organisation, membership and image, and to rethink some of our policies," Hague told party activists during the contest. Clarke won 70 votes.
Hague, the youngest cabinet minister for 50 years when he became Welsh Secretary in 1995, is a relative newcomer to the political spotlight but he has been a media star since 1977.

At that year's Conservative party conference the 16-year-old Hague impressed Margaret Thatcher and brought the 5,000 delegates to their feet with a rousing speech calling on the then-Labour government to "roll back the frontiers of the state".

Many of the right-wing ideas he put forward in that speech became pillars of Thatcher's philosophy. She stepped into the fight at the last minute on Wednesday to support Hague against Clarke, whose pro-European views she mistrusts.

Hague graduated from Oxford with a first class degree in philosophy, politics and economics, and initially became a press officer for oil giant Shell before joining the McKinsey management consultancy.

It was no surprise when Hague, who was hooked on politics from an early age, decided to contest the Richmond seat in north Yorkshire in 1989. Born in Yorkshire, Hague was the only son of the owner of a soft drinks business and was the first cabinet minister to attend a comprehensive state school.

Hague's rise to cabinet status, via ministerial posts in the social security department, was swift but left few outside or inside parliament with much idea of what he stood for or which wing of the party he represented.
During the campaign he mouthed little but platitudes about key areas of policy, except Europe, in an apparent attempt -- Major-like -- to appeal to as many Conservative MPs as possible.

Before the election, his views on the key issue of Europe were thought to be neither pro- nor anti-. After announcing his candidacy, Hague progressively moved towards the "Eurosceptics" in his party, finally ruling out joining a single currency last Thursday.

This led to accusations Hague was fitting his political views into whatever straitjacket was needed to achieve victory. His enemies condemned his lack of backbone as well as a perceived lack of clear ideas -- a clone of Major in other words.
"He is a man of quality yet a man without qualities; his political personality is not just indistinct but undetectable," said former Conservative MP George Walden.
Clarke was the favourite of ordinary Conservative supporters, who could not vote in the contest, because of his experience and hard-hitting parliamentary style.

But supporters say the prematurely balding Hague is a man of vision, much tougher than he looks and is capable of uniting his fractious colleagues. The man himself scoffs at comparisons with Major with whom he shares a warming smile and an ability to get on with almost everyone.
He says he will be his own man with his own ideas, and will reimpose discipline in a party that almost tore itself apart before the election over the issue of closer ties with the European Union.
"I'm not going to live my life as a comparison with any previous leader - I am going to be myself," he said.
Hague maintains "I've finally got past the point where people say 'Oh, you're that teenager'", but for many MPs the prematurely balding Hague remains a youngster still untested under fire.

He took a step towards updating his image as a "young fogey" by announcing shortly before the election he would marry Ffion Jenkins, a 29-year-old civil servant high-flyer he met when she taught him the words to the Welsh national anthem.
